feedback: For a sample with one quarter of its parent remaining, confirm two half-lives have passed and multiply by the half-life for the age.
If a learner selects carbon-14 for a 100-million-year rock, remind them carbon-14 is exhausted beyond ~50,000 years and a long-lived system is required.
When ordering by age, check reasoning uses the ratio consistently rather than absolute counts.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the decay model is understood, the parent:daughter ratio and half-life give a calculable age, and the appropriate isotope depends on both the material and the timescale.
learnerActions: Given a parent:daughter ratio and a half-life, set or write the number of half-lives and the approximate age (e.g. one quarter of parent left and a 1.3-billion-year half-life → two half-lives → ~2.6 billion years).

Answer which isotope system would date a stated material: e.g. which clock for a 100-million-year igneous rock (uranium-lead or potassium-argon), and which for a few-thousand-year-old piece of wood or bone (carbon-14).
Order a set of samples from youngest to oldest from their parent:daughter ratios (more daughter relative to parent = older, for the same isotope).
activities.title: Compute the age and match the clock

feedback: If a learner thinks the bone itself is dated, clarify that the surrounding volcanic rock is usually dated to bracket the fossil's age.
Reinforce that matching clock to timescale, not the age of the object alone, drives method choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Carbon-14's ~50,000-year range is far too short for 66-million-year fossils, and fossils are typically dated by bracketing igneous/ash layers whose minerals suit long-lived isotope systems.
learnerActions: Pose the question 'Why can't you carbon-date a dinosaur bone?' and read or discuss the explanation.
Explore the follow-up: why scientists usually date volcanic ash layers above and below a fossil rather than the fossil itself.
Summarise in their own words what is actually being dated and why the choice of isotope matters.
activities.title: Ask the geochronologist: why not carbon-date a T. rex?
